To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(a) explaining why a negative workplace event occurred (e.g., why a layoff occurred) can enhance perceptions of justice and positive views of an organization among people at higher levels of abstract construal, but (b) explaining how a negative workplace event was implemented (e.g., how layoff recipients will be treated with respect) can enhance perceptions justice and positive views among people at lower levels of concrete construal.
When explaining why or how it happens is more effective depends on the level of construal.
providing accounts for organizational events is more effective when the account is tailored to the observer's construal level.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of providing explanations for negative organizational events.
how people react to negative events that happen at work and how organizations can respond to these events.
how organizations communicate with employees about negative workplace decisions and how these communications are perceived by employees.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the results show how and why accounts are more effective under certain conditions, and this study has shown that the results are consistent with construal level theory.

the findings of the present study indicate that accounts focusing on why an event occurred are more effective when observers are at a higher level of construal, while accounts focusing on how an event occurred are effective when observers are lower in construal.

the results of the study show that accounts of why a negative organizational decision was made are more effective for people at higher levels of abstract thinking, whereas accounts of how a negative organizational decision is implemented are more effective at lower levels of abstract thinking.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the effectiveness of different types of explanations for negative organizational decisions depends on observers' construal levels.
we show how and why people's perceptions and reactions are influenced by the level of abstraction they are in when they receive information about a negative organizational decision.
we show that the effectiveness of accounts for organizational decisions is moderated by construal level.
